To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Ca(2+), Sr(2+), Mn(2+), and Ba(2+) shift the cAMP dose-response curve for activation of cAMP- gated channels to the right, whereas Mg(2+) has no effect.
the cAMP-gating of cyclic nucleotide-gates of olfactory receptor cells is modulated by divalent cations and that this modulation may depend on previous preexposure to other divalents.
Ca2+ and Sr2+, at low concentrations, cause a decrease in the affinity of the cAMP-binding site in the cAMP-gate channel.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms underlying the transduction of olfactory receptor cell responses to odorants.
the role of calcium ions in the olfactory transduction process, in particular, in the desensitisation of the olfactory response.
the role of Ca2+ and calmodulin in the regulation of the cyclic AMP-gated channels of olfactory receptor cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
divalent cations are not only important for channel gating, but also modulate the channel response to cAMP, and this modulation depends on the previous exposure to other divalent ions.
the cyclic nucleotide-gating channels are modulated by Ca2+, but the exact nature of the modulation is still unknown.
the binding of Ca2+, Sr2+ and Mn2+ to the cyclic nucleotide binding sites of the channel protein, probably via a protein, controls the affinity of the binding of cAMP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cAMP-gating of the olfactory cationic channels is controlled by the interaction between the channel protein and a regulatory protein, which may be calmodulin, or a protein with calmodulin-like properties.

the cyclic nucleotide-gating channels in olfactory receptor cells are under the control of divalent cation-dependent regulatory proteins, and this may be a mechanism for the desensitisation of the odorant-induced response.
the cAMP-gating mechanism is a complex one, involving several proteins and divalent cations in a sequence-dependent manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Ca(2+) affinity of the cAMP binding site of the olfactory cyclic nucleotide-gating channel can be controlled by the presence of Ca(2+) and Mg(2+) in the cytoplasm.
the binding of divalents, likely via a regulatory protein (calmodulin), controls the sensitivity of cAMP-gated olfactory channels to cAMP.
divalent cations can control the affinity of cyclic nucleotide-gating channels to their ligands.
